h1: Jobs in an Indian winery, from cellar hand to winemaker
title: Jobs in an Indian Winery | Craft Beer School
desc: The jobs inside an Indian winery, from vineyard and cellar hand to lab technician and winemaker, with what each role does through the year.
teaser: Harvest in Nashik runs while most of the world's vineyards are resting. Here is who does what in an Indian winery.
standfirst: Indian wineries are small teams with a busy few months at harvest and steady work the rest of the year. This guide walks through the roles, from cellar hand to winemaker, with what each one involves.
sections: How an Indian winery year works

Most Indian wine comes from Maharashtra, around Nashik, with Karnataka the other main region. Indian vineyards are usually pruned twice a year. The crop is grown through the cooler, drier months. Harvest generally falls between January and April, the opposite of the European autumn. Our guide to Indian wine regions explains why.

That calendar shapes the jobs. Harvest and crush are intense, with long days and extra hands. The rest of the year is quieter cellar work: fermentation, ageing, blending, filtering and bottling, plus tasting room and sales activity.

Some wineries own vineyards, others buy grapes from contract farmers. Many do both. Vineyard roles include field workers, vineyard supervisors and viticulturists.

A viticulturist advises on pruning, canopy management, irrigation, pest and disease control and when to pick. Picking decisions rely on sampling grapes for sugar, measured in degrees Brix, along with acidity and taste. Table wine grapes are often picked somewhere around 22 to 24 °Brix, though the target depends on the style. A viticulturist usually has an agriculture or horticulture background.

The cellar hand is the entry role in the winery itself. The work is physical: receiving grapes, running the crusher and press, moving must and wine between tanks, cleaning everything, topping up barrels and helping on the bottling line.

Cleaning takes up a large share of the day, because wine spoils easily if equipment is dirty. It is good training. You learn how every piece of kit works and see each stage of winemaking up close. Many winemakers started as cellar hands.

Every winery runs basic analysis. The lab technician measures sugar, alcohol, pH, total acidity and sulphur dioxide, checks fermentations each day and tests wine before bottling. Free sulphur dioxide matters a lot, because it protects wine from oxidation and microbes. Levels drift as wine ages.

This role suits graduates in chemistry, microbiology or food technology. It is also a strong route towards winemaking, because the lab sees every tank.

The assistant winemaker supervises cellar work, runs fermentations day to day and helps with blending and planning. The winemaker sets the style of the wines, decides when to pick, chooses yeasts and fermentation temperatures, plans blends and signs off every wine before bottling.

Indian winemakers often have formal training in oenology, sometimes from programmes abroad, alongside several vintages of practical work. Some wineries also bring in visiting consultant winemakers during harvest. If you want to see the process the winemaker manages, our guide to how wine is made covers it step by step.

• Bottling line operator: runs the filler, corker or capper and labeller.
  • Quality and compliance staff: manage records for food safety and excise, which vary by state.
  • Tasting room and hospitality: wine tourism around Nashik and Bengaluru has grown. Tasting rooms need staff who can guide visitors.
  • Sales and marketing: selling to hotels, restaurants and retailers across states with different rules.
What winery work feels like day to day

During harvest a cellar shift can start before sunrise, when grapes arrive cool from the vineyard. It can run late into the evening as presses empty and tanks fill. Fermenting tanks need checking at least daily for temperature and sugar. Red wine tanks need the cap of skins pushed down or pumped over so colour and flavour are extracted. Weekends do not exist for a few weeks.

Outside harvest the pace is calmer and more regular. Work moves to racking wine off its sediment, topping up barrels, filtering, blending trials and bottling runs. Heat is a constant concern in India, so much of the cellar work is about keeping wine cool and protected from oxygen.

Harvest is the best entry point. Wineries need extra hands every season and a good harvest worker is often asked back. Contact wineries well before harvest, because staffing is planned ahead.

If you come from brewing, many skills carry over: hygiene, fermentation management, lab work and sensory evaluation. Our overview of jobs in a brewery shows how similar the structure is. What differs is the raw material. Grapes arrive once a year and every decision at harvest stays in the wine. Understanding why winemakers make the choices they do is the most useful thing to learn before your first vintage.
faqs: When is harvest season in Indian wineries?
Generally between January and April, depending on the region and the variety. This is the busiest time for winery staff.
Do I need a degree to work in an Indian winery?
Not for cellar hand or harvest work. Lab and winemaking roles usually ask for a science degree, often with training in oenology.
Can a brewer move into winemaking?
Yes. Fermentation, hygiene and lab skills carry over. The main things to learn are grape growing, harvest decisions and wine specific processes such as pressing and ageing.
